newsitem.title: USA: Once burned twice shy, dlr pros bet on more gains.
newsitem.headline: Once burned twice shy, dlr pros bet on more gains.

text.p: Widespread fear of missing out on a second liftoff will propel the dollar higher against the mark, after the dollar caught most currency dealers off guard and rocketed to a near two-year high on Tuesday, analysts said.
The dollar rose to a peak of 1.5735 marks on Tuesday from 1.50 marks less than 10 trading sessions ago before falling back to around 1.5555 by midafternoon.
Fear of missing the rich rewards of any follow-up rally helps boost the odds of a continuation of the dollar's recent march higher, strategists said on Tuesday.
"The fear of missing an explosive move is outweighing the fear of chasing the dollar," said Marc Chandler, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"I think for this whole month of December, we should be looking for the dollar to trend higher," he added.
David Durrant, senior currency strategist at I.D.E.A., forecast a dollar rise to around 1.58 marks before the year-end holidays.
"We had squeezed out a lot of long money over the past months. They stayed out for a while and now are willing to jump back in because they don't want to miss out," Durrant said.
"It would not appear to us that the market is in any way, shape, or form overbought at this point," Durrant added.
However, some remain skeptical, noting the dollar's rise was triggered by technical factors and official comments, not by any meaningful fundamental economic news.
In addition, the dollar suffers each time doubts arise over European Union member states' ability to meet strict EMU convergence criteria in 1997, analysts said.
"You can't read too much into these sharp dollar swings. There was no real shift in fundamentals this week or even last month," said David Gilmore, partner at Foreign Exchange Analytics.
"I think (dollar/mark) is probably nearing the top. We might get another spurt higher, like we saw over the last two days, but I can't imagine it getting much above 1.60."

Recent comments from German and U.S. officials underpinned the spike in the U.S. unit. The remarks fed a growing expectation that European and U.S. officials will continue, and perhaps even strengthen, their cries for a strong dollar, analysts said.

A rising dollar would aid those nations seeking to meet economic criteria in order to join the proposed European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), by promoting exports and thus bolstering their domestic economies.

The dollar hit a fresh 23-month peak against the mark and Swiss franc on Tuesday after Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing predicted a shift from marks to dollars and New York Federal Reserve Bank President William McDonough said the dollar's reserve currency status would become more important as EMU approached in 1999.
While market makers said the dollar was being pushed higher by official comments, UK Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Tuesday it was all in the market's hands.
"I actually don't think that (EU) member states have the complete control over these exchange rates in the way in which others imagine. The market...determines these things," he said.
But dealers do not expect a further rise in the dollar against European currencies to spark any official backlash.

When asked whether he expects to see U.S. officials waver from their longstanding strong dollar policy, Durrant said: "Not in the near term. I think if we see the dollar go to 1.70 (marks) we might have (US Treasury Secretary) Robert Rubin come out and say it's gone too far."
-- Roanne Daniels, 212-859-1677
